The Quad’s work does not stop between summits
Credibility of the grouping will rest on what it delivers for the wider Indo-Pacific, not on how often its leaders meet.

After a two-year gap, the leaders of the Quad have finally met in Manila on the sidelines of the 2026 ASEAN Summit. The delay had fuelled speculation about the grouping’s future, with suggestions that it was losing relevance or might eventually fade into irrelevance. The summit challenges that assessment.

All four countries continue to see strategic value in the partnership, despite differences in their priorities and the absence of a regular leaders’ meeting. But the issue is whether these leaders’ meetings can help strengthen the Quad’s institutional mechanisms and ensure that cooperation continues to advance between summits.

Notwithstanding the importance of leaders’ summits because of the need for a political direction, they are not where most of its substantive work takes place. Cooperation is sustained through ministerial engagements, official-level consultations, and specialised working groups. The two-year gap, therefore, should not be read as evidence of the Quad’s inactivity. In fact, despite the Quad’s accountability gap, this focus on summit diplomacy overlooks the work the Quad has continued through its ministerial and official-level mechanisms.
The continuity of the partnership depends on their ability to sustain cooperation between leaders’ meetings.

The Quad’s informal structure allows the four countries to work together on issues where they share common interests, without requiring them to settle their differences on other matters first. This flexibility is needed because India, Japan, Australia, and the United States do not always see regional and international developments in the same way. They can, however, continue working together on specific areas of mutual interest through ministerial meetings and official-level engagements, even when their leaders are not meeting regularly.

The continuity of the partnership depends on their ability to sustain cooperation between leaders’ meetings. Strengthening these ministerial and official-level processes, ensuring regular engagement, and translating political commitments into concrete initiatives should therefore be a priority for the four countries.

The Manila joint statement illustrates why the work undertaken between summits matters far more than the gap between them. The proposed Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration, particularly the announcement that P-8 and P-3C patrol aircraft are expected to participate in a maritime exercise in 2027, gives the grouping’s maritime cooperation a more operational dimension. This builds on its longstanding focus on maritime domain awareness but also requires sustained coordination among defence officials and maritime agencies. The progress of such cooperation cannot be measured by leaders’ meetings alone.

A second important development is the Quad’s growing attention to critical infrastructure. Progress under the Partnership for Cable Connectivity and Resilience is an understanding that regional security also depends on protecting the infrastructure underpinning digital and economic connectivity. But the Quad’s regional credibility will depend on whether these initiatives benefit countries beyond its four members. The task ahead is to translate cooperation into outcomes for the wider Indo-Pacific, which requires strong institution-building by the Quad.

The joint statement also reiterates support for ASEAN centrality and unity, a free and open Indo-Pacific, and cooperation against terrorism and violent extremism. These commitments provide political continuity, but regional countries will judge the partnership by more than its declarations. They will want to know whether its initiatives address their practical concerns, whether they can participate in them, and whether the benefits extend beyond the four members. This includes support for maritime surveillance and the protection of their exclusive economic zones, investment in resilient infrastructure and digital connectivity, and access to technology and cybersecurity capabilities. The Quad has an opportunity to strengthen its standing in the region through maritime capacity-building, infrastructure resilience, and technological cooperation. The fact that the four members share strategic interests does not necessarily mean that other countries in the region will share their enthusiasm for the Quad.

These initiatives require sustained political backing. Leaders’ meetings can reaffirm priorities and give officials the mandate to take cooperation forward, but they cannot substitute for the work that follows. The proposed business forum, maritime exercise, and infrastructure projects will be developed and implemented through engagements at lower levels. Their progress will not depend on whether the four leaders meet again next year, but on whether their governments continue to commit resources and attention to them.

The Quad should therefore be judged by what it delivers in between leaders’ meetings. The Manila summit does not by itself prove that the grouping has suddenly become more effective. In any case, the demands of contemporary global politics dictate that world leaders have far too many summits in their over-stretched calendars. The Manila meeting has reaffirmed political commitment and provided direction to an expanding agenda. Whether it strengthens the Quad will depend on implementation, and, crucially, on whether its initiatives produce results that matter to the wider Indo-Pacific.
